title: Cab's strict punctuality and Francis's dream of playing with Duke
summary: Cab's businesslike bandstand taught him to be on time; he had listened to Duke on a crystal set in Miami and later replaced Louis Bellson.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Not only that, but that experience in that band paid off for me later on when I went in the studio, that I was never late, because in Cab's band, he was strictly business. In that band, off that bandstand, he was Cab, but on the bandstand, he was Mr. Calloway. There was no foolishness going on; if you were supposed to hit at 9 o'clock, 15 minutes to 9, he was on the bandstand picking out the tunes that we were gonna play, and at 9 o'clock, he did not look up to see whether you were there or not, he brought his hands down.

And that's how I learned about making time, which-- I loved Duke, and I had the greatest respect for Duke Ellington, because I thought he was -- well, in fact, not thought, but I think he is the greatest thing that ever lived. Because when I was a kid down in Miami, I used to have my little

crystal set, and I used to hear his band from the Cotton Club, and I always dreamed that one day I'd probably get a chance to play in his band -- which did happen when Louis Bellson went to England to marry Pearl Bailey; I took his place in the band.
Oh, you did? You got a chance to play with him.
